notes: v2.114 (2026-11-18, evening run): 113th tower 'Christmas Tree' (a star over widening tiers on a trunk — a Christmas tree silhouette to demolish, 18 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 4/5/4/3/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 110th co-play prompt (decorate a tree together — hang big soft ornaments on the low branches saying 'up… on!', take them off again saying 'off… again!', and let Liam choose where each one goes; soft, shatterproof ornaments on low branches only, glass/hooks/tiny parts stay up high with a grown-up, a felt tree on the wall works just as well). Christmas-tree-decorating research: placing and removing ornaments on low branches builds fine motor and hand-eye coordination and pride/belonging ('my ornament on the tree'), and the off-and-on loop is the mastery game — a felt tree lets him decorate again and again. v2.113 (2026-11-18, morning run): 112th tower 'Sleigh' (a tall backrest and gift pile over a wide body and rail on two runner feet — a sleigh side profile to demolish, 28 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 6/5/6/7/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 109th co-play prompt (take a sleigh ride together — a grown-up pulls Liam slowly across the floor in a laundry basket saying 'ho… ho… here we go!', then swap and let him pull the basket with a soft toy inside saying 'pull… pull!'; take turns riding and pulling, flat floor, slow and steady, no stairs, no tipping). Sleigh-play research: pulling is cause-and-effect plus gross motor (pull → it follows), loading and hauling builds planning and fine motor, and riding in turns is the social form. Block Pop replaced the 9-activity menu game on 2026-10-13 (kept as classic.html). One deep mechanic: tap a color cannon, blast matching block clusters, clear the tower. v2.112 (2026-11-17, evening run): 111th tower 'Cookie' (a round cookie with chocolate chips — indented top and bottom over wide middle bands with a three-chip centre row, 21 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 3/7/3/5/3, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 108th co-play prompt (bake cookies together — stir the dough saying 'stir… stir!', pat it flat and press in chocolate chips saying 'press… press!', count the first three chips — one, two, three! — then leave two cookies and a little cup of milk out for Santa saying 'for Santa!', and take a bite of your own cookie together; take turns; a grown-up picks the recipe and checks for allergies first, and handles the oven and the hot tray; little hands do the stirring, patting, and pressing, and the dough is for baking, not for eating raw). Cookie/baking-play research: at 2, baking is a full-body developmental activity — scooping flour needs hand-eye coordination, stirring thick dough builds wrist and forearm strength, rolling and pressing builds bilateral coordination, and picking up a sprinkle or placing a chocolate chip is pincer grasp, the same muscles later used for holding a pencil; the kitchen is a sensory lab (flour's silkiness vs. sugar's grain, cinnamon and vanilla smells), and counting scoops or chips together is early numeracy kept to the 1–3 range; the honest toddler form is high-success jobs only (dump, stir, press, sprinkle) with everything pre-measured and a grown-up on the oven — and leaving milk and cookies out for Santa is the giving ritual that ties the prompt to the Santa tower (v2.89). Pivot note: this run first drafted a Stocking tower + prompt, then caught that Stocking is already the 85th tower (v2.86, 2026-11-09) with its own hide-and-find prompt — both were reverted before shipping and the batch pivoted to Cookie, the same Turkey-lesson discipline as v2.84 and the Menorah run; the stocking-schema search was still useful (enveloping/containing schema — stuff things in, pull them out, object permanence), but its takeaways were already logged in the 2026-11-09 Stocking note. Continues the December series at home after Wreath, Ornament, Snowflake, Bell, Candy Cane, Dreidel, Menorah and Chimney. v2.111 (2026-11-17, afternoon run): 110th tower 'Chimney' (a smoke puff over a brick stack on a wide base — a chimney silhouette to demolish, 24 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 6/4/4/4/6, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 107th co-play prompt (build a real chimney from big blocks (or a cardboard tube) together — stack them up saying 'up… up… up!', drop a big soft pom-pom down the top saying 'down it goes!', watch it pop out the bottom saying 'there it is!', and drop it again — in the top, out the bottom is the game; take turns; big soft pom-poms or a soft ball only, nothing small enough to fit in a mouth, a grown-up holds the chimney steady; that's how Santa comes down the chimney — down it goes, ho ho ho!). Chimney/drop-play research: dropping balls or pom-poms down an inclined tube and watching them fall out the bottom is canonical cause-and-effect + object-permanence play at 2 (toddler learning guidelines: drop balls in an inclined tube, watch them fall to the bottom, then put them back at the top to repeat; a pom-pom drop wall is a toddler favourite — tape paper tubes to a wall at angles, basket at the bottom, drop and watch; passing objects through a tube reinforces that things still exist even when you can't see them). Continues the December series at home after Wreath, Ornament, Snowflake, Bell, Candy Cane, Dreidel and Menorah. v2.110 (2026-11-17, morning run): 109th tower 'Menorah' (two outer candles over sweeping arms, a centre stem and a wide base — a candelabra silhouette to demolish, 19 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 2/2/2/2/4/7, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 106th co-play prompt (light a pretend menorah together — stand nine little candles in a row, paper tubes or chunky blocks, the middle one the helper candle; count the first three — one, two, three! — then pretend to light each one with the helper candle saying 'light… light!', and hold your hands over the glow saying 'warm… warm!'; take turns; pretend candles only — no real flames, a grown-up lights any real candles, battery candles are the safe ones for little hands). Menorah/Hanukkah-play research: toddlers never handle real fire — the honest form is a felt/toy/paper menorah or battery candles, 'lit' by placing a paper flame or tissue on each candle; counting candles is the math — one more each night, counted aloud by the parent, kept to the 1–3 subitizing range in the prompt while nine stays a parent fact; the shamash helper candle that lights the others is the social beat; dimming the lights and sitting close to watch the glow is the built-in calm settle. Pivot note: this run first drafted a Snowman tower + prompt, then caught that Snowman is already the 76th tower (v2.72, 2026-11-06) with its own prompt — both were reverted before shipping and the batch pivoted to Menorah, the same Turkey-lesson discipline as v2.84 and the Whale run. Hanukkah 2026 begins at sundown Fri Dec 4 — the second Hanukkah tower after Dreidel, completing the pair ahead of the holiday. v2.109 (2026-11-16, evening run): 108th tower 'Dreidel' (a handle over a square body tapering to a point — two yellow stem blocks over red, blue and green bands on a green point, 17 blocks, 4 clusters sizes 2/4/4/7, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 105th co-play prompt (spin a dreidel together — hold a big dreidel by its handle and twist it saying 'spin… spin!', watch it go round and round, then wait for it to wobble and fall down saying 'down it goes!'; take turns; at 2 the game is just spin and watch it fall — no rules, no little coins or candy — and a grown-up holds any small dreidel; a big wooden dreidel or a chunky spinning top works best). Dreidel/spinning-play research: spinning is the rotation schema — toddlers are fascinated by circular motion, and a spin teaches force, speed, direction and visual tracking, with the spin-then-fall as a built-in calm settle; the dreidel game itself suits 3+ with supervision, so at 2 the honest form is spin-and-watch-it-fall only, no rules and no gelt; spinning tops are suitable from around age 2 when large, safe and rounded, and the twist builds pincer grip and wrist strength. Hanukkah 2026 begins at sundown Fri Dec 4 and ends at nightfall Sat Dec 12 — the first non-Christmas December tower, widening the December series beyond Wreath, Ornament, Snowflake, Bell and Candy Cane. v2.108 (2026-11-16, afternoon run): 107th tower 'Candy Cane' (a hook over a striped stick — top bar and curl over alternating red/yellow/blue/green bands on a red base, 16 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 8/2/2/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 104th co-play prompt (twist a candy cane together — twist red and white pipe cleaners round and round saying 'twist… twist!', bend the top over into a hook, then hang it on a low branch by its hook saying 'hang… hang!', take it off, and hang it again — off and on is the game; take turns; a grown-up twists the pipe cleaners with you — a real candy cane can break sharp, so the pretend one is for twisting and hanging). Candy-cane-play research: the hook's physics is the headline — the hook was designed to hang on trees, so hanging by the hook (and taking it off and hanging it again) is the canonical play; red/white stripes are a pattern to decode — twisting red and white pipe cleaners into stripes is fine-motor patterning at 2; stirring cocoa with a real cane is the classic use, but the Cocoa prompt already covers stirring a cup, so this prompt keeps the twist-and-hook-hang, which no prior prompt covers. Continues the December series at home after Wreath, Ornament, Snowflake and Bell. v2.107 (2026-11-16, morning run): 106th tower 'Bell' (a bow-topped bell — two bow loops over a knot, a tapering dome, a wide skirt, a bottom band and a hanging clapper, 28 blocks, 7 clusters sizes 2/2/4/6/6/6/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 103rd co-play prompt (ring a little bell together — hold it by the handle and shake it saying 'ring… ring!', then shake it fast, then slow, then hold it still with both hands and listen quietly — can you hear it stop? Take turns; one small bell at a time, a grown-up holds it if it is small, and if the ringing gets too loud, hold it quiet together and listen instead). Bell-play research: shake-and-stop is the core skill (Purdue ELM) — the hand makes the sound and the hand makes the quiet, building self-regulation and cause-effect; fast vs. slow shaking changes the sound, so the contrast itself teaches cause-and-effect; bells can overstimulate some toddlers, so the honest form is one bell, one at a time, gentle, with a quiet-listening alternative. Continues the December series at home after Wreath, Ornament and Snowflake. v2.106 (2026-11-15, evening run): 105th tower 'Snowflake' (a six-armed flake — top arm, side arms, and two diagonal bottom arms over a centre, 23 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 5/4/4/4/3/3, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 102nd co-play prompt (make a real paper snowflake together — fold a coffee filter in half, then in half again, a grown-up snips a few little shapes along the folded edges saying 'snip… snip!', then open it up slowly together saying 'ta-da!' — every snowflake comes out different! Hang it in the window to catch the light; take turns; at 2 the fun is the big unfold reveal, and tearing white paper into pieces and sticking them on is the no-scissors way to play). Snowflake-play research: the unfold is the payoff — fold, snip, unfold, gasp — and every snowflake is different, which builds pride; simple folded cutting works from about age 4, so at 2 the grown-up folds and snips while the child does the unfold reveal and the decorating; six-fold symmetry is early geometry a parent can name ('whatever you snip shows up all around!') with no counting demand; coffee filters and lightweight paper are easiest on little hands. Continues the December series at home after Wreath and Ornament. v2.105 (2026-11-15, afternoon run): 104th tower 'Ornament' (a hook loop over a cap and a round ball body, 22 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 2/4/6/6/4, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 101st co-play prompt (decorate one big soft ornament together — stick big stickers on it saying 'stick… stick!', hang it on a low branch saying 'hang… hang!', then take it off and hang it again — off and on is the game; take turns; soft felt, wood, or foam ornaments only, on low branches, no glass, no sharp hooks, a grown-up handles the lights and cords). Ornament-play research: at 2, decorating a plain wooden/foam ornament with big stickers is the canonical craft — peeling stickers and pinching shapes builds fine motor and colour recognition, and seeing his own ornament on the tree builds pride and belonging; pulling ornaments off is itself the play — a dangling ornament is a cause-and-effect experiment (pull → falls or makes a noise), so the off-and-on loop is the mastery game, not a misbehaviour; the honest toddler form is soft ornaments on low branches only, glass/ceramic excluded, nothing above waist height. Continues the December series after Wreath, with the family home from the trip today. v2.104 (2026-11-15, morning run): 103rd tower 'Wreath' (red berries over a green ring with a blue band and a yellow bow, 24 blocks, 8 clusters sizes 3/5/2/2/2/2/5/3, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 100th co-play prompt (make a real paper-plate wreath together — trace the round ring saying 'round… round!', tear green paper and stick it all around saying 'stick… stick!', add big red pom-poms, and hang it on the door together saying 'ta-da!'; take turns; a grown-up does the cutting and the hanging, non-toxic glue stick and big pieces only, no small bits in mouths, and hang it where he can see it and point at it together). Wreath-play research: at 2, the paper-plate ring is the canonical toddler wreath — a grown-up cuts the centre out, the child tears paper and sticks it all around (fine motor, pincer grasp, red/green colour sorting); the circle itself is early geometry, traced 'round and round' with a finger; hanging it on the door is the payoff, and the grown-up does the cutting and the hanging. Timed to the trip's end — the family flies home today (Sun Nov 15, WN2895 SAN 10:45 AM), so this is the first December-series tower after the trip, resuming the Christmas set (Tree, Stocking, Present, Reindeer, Santa, Elf, Gingerbread) with a home-for-the-holidays craft. v2.103 (2026-11-14, evening run): 102nd tower 'Suitcase' (a handle over three wide body bands on two wheels, 26 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 6/6/6/4/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 99th co-play prompt (pack a little bag together — choose a few soft toys, put each one in saying 'in… in!', zip it shut saying 'zip… zip!', carry it around the room, then open it up and take everything out again saying 'out… out!'; take turns; a small bag or backpack with soft toys only, a grown-up helps with the zip, and pack it for the trip home tomorrow). Packing-play research: at 2, putting things in and taking them out is the containing schema — filling bags and boxes teaches space, size, and fit, and in/out and full/empty are early-math words; packing a bag (choose, put in, close, carry, unpack) is early sequencing, and unpacking-and-repacking is the mastery payoff. Timed to the trip — the family flies home tomorrow (Sun Nov 15, WN2895 SAN 10:45 AM), so the tower lands on packing-up night, the same trip-timing as Airplane (flight day), Starfish (aquarium-and-beach day), and Sandcastle (beach day). v2.102 (2026-11-14, afternoon run): 101st tower 'Sandcastle' (a flag over a battlement top and two wide body bands on two base towers, 23 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 6/6/5/2/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 98th co-play prompt (build a real sandcastle together at Kellogg Park beach — scoop wet sand into a bucket saying 'scoop… scoop!', pat it down, tip the bucket over and lift it off saying 'ta-da!', then knock the castle down together saying 'crash… down!' and build it again; take turns scooping and patting; stay close to your grown-up near the water, and keep sand out of eyes and mouths; look for shells in the sand together). Sand-play research: at 2, scooping, pouring, and packing sand builds fine motor and hand-eye coordination and teaches full/empty and wet/dry cause-and-effect; building then knocking down is the payoff — toddlers love flattening sand pies and castles and starting over (DK Baby's First Skills; Goric); sand play is calming and open-ended with no right way, and a collapse teaches rebuild-and-adapt resilience. Timed to the trip — the family is at Kellogg Park beach this afternoon (Sat Nov 14), so the tower lands on the actual beach stop, the same trip-timing as Starfish (aquarium-and-beach day), Jellyfish (aquarium-eve), Seal/Whale (SeaWorld day), and Brick/Pirate (LEGOLAND day). v2.101 (2026-11-14, morning run): 100th tower 'Starfish' (a top arm over a wide side-arm band and two lower arms, 22 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 4/2/3/2/11, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 97th co-play prompt (be a starfish together — lie down and stretch arms and legs out wide saying 'star… star!', count its five arms together — one, two, three, four, five — then curl up small like a sleepy starfish and rest; take turns; pretend only, no real water, real starfish are look, don't touch; at Birch Aquarium, watch the starfish in the tide pools, and at the beach, look for one in the sand and leave it where it lives). Starfish-play research: at 2, most sea stars have 5 arms and counting them with fingers is the natural toddler entry — the parent counts aloud while Liam points/touches (early-math note); the star pose is whole-body (arms and legs out wide, then curl small), distinct from the Star tower's finger twinkles; tide pools are look-and-gentle-touch only where the aquarium invites it, and beach starfish stay where they live. Jellyfish-play research: at 2, the jellyfish move is arms hanging loose and wiggling like tentacles (Ocean Animal Yoga) — the 'Jellyfish Jiggle' is drop your hands, wiggle, wave your arms about; bobbing up high and dipping down low is the up/down drift, and floating and resting is the settle; real jellyfish can sting, so the safety line is watch from a safe distance and never touch. Timed to the trip — the family visits Birch Aquarium tomorrow (Sat Nov 14), so the tower lands the day before the aquarium visit, the same trip-timing as Dolphin (SeaWorld-eve), Shark (SeaWorld-eve), and Octopus (SeaWorld-eve). v2.99 (2026-11-13, afternoon run): 98th tower 'Whale' (a spout over a head and a wide body on two tail flukes, 28 blocks, 6 clusters sizes 2/8/7/7/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 95th co-play prompt (be a big blue whale together — stretch arms out wide saying 'big… big!', sway side to side saying 'sway… sway!', dive down low, come back up and blow your spout — point to the top of your head and thrust your arms up saying 'whoosh!', then float and rest like a sleepy whale; take turns; pretend only, no real water, real whales are look, don't touch; at SeaWorld, watch the whales splash and spout together). Whale-play research: at 2, the spout is the signature move ('I'm a Great Big Whale' — point to the blowhole on top of the head, flip the tail as you dive down, then come up and thrust arms up with a big 'WHOOSH!' — a blowing game that builds breath control); 'whales are very big' (stretch arms out wide) is the big/small entry language; dive-down-then-up is the up/down cycle with a float-and-rest settle. Timed to the SeaWorld trip — the family is at SeaWorld today (Fri Nov 13), so the tower lands on the actual park day, the same trip-timing as Pirate (park day), Brick (park day), and Seal (park day). v2.98 (2026-11-13, morning run): 97th tower 'Seal' (a ball balanced on a seal's head over a wide body on two tail flippers, 28 blocks, 4 clusters sizes 2/8/7/11, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 94th co-play prompt (be a seal together — clap your hands like seal flippers saying 'clap… clap!', bark like a seal saying 'arf… arf!', then balance a soft ball on your head like a seal balances a ball on its nose — hold still… then let it drop and clap again, and rest like a sleepy seal; take turns; pretend only, no real water, real seals are look, don't touch; at SeaWorld, watch the seals clap their flippers together). Seal-play research: at 2, 'if you want to be a seal, clap your flippers!' is the canonical toddler action-song move (Zoo Animals, to 'If You're Happy and You Know It'); clapping games like pat-a-cake are a core 1–2 rhythm/imitation form; imitating animal movements builds gross-motor skills, balance, and flexibility, starting with moves the child can already do; the seal act is balancing a ball on the nose (Goki push-along seal, Sonny the Seal barks and claps on success) — a copyable balance-and-drop moment. Timed to the SeaWorld trip — the family is at SeaWorld today (Fri Nov 13), so the tower lands on the actual park day, the same trip-timing as Pirate (park day) and Brick (park day). v2.97 (2026-11-12, evening run): 96th tower 'Octopus' (round head over two wide body bands with four dangling arms, 30 blocks, 7 clusters sizes 8/7/7/2/2/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 93rd co-play prompt (be an octopus together — wiggle your arms like wiggly octopus arms saying 'wiggle… wiggle!', spin around slowly, touch the ground, then rest like a sleepy octopus; take turns; an octopus has eight arms — count the first three together: one, two, three!; pretend only, no real water, real octopuses are look, don't touch; at SeaWorld, look for the octopus waving its arms together). Octopus-play research: at 2, 'wiggle 8 arms like an octopus' is the canonical sea-animal movement (feet planted, arms only, waving like tentacles); the octopus fingerplay/song is spin around, touch the ground, wiggle eight arms, squirt your ink — adapted here as wiggle + slow spin + touch ground + rest, with the ink-squirt dropped as too abstract and the counting kept to the 1–3 subitizing range. Timed to the SeaWorld trip — the family visits SeaWorld tomorrow (Fri Nov 13), so the tower lands the day before, the same trip-timing as Dolphin (SeaWorld-eve) and Shark (SeaWorld-eve). v2.96 (2026-11-12, afternoon run): 95th tower 'Shark' (dorsal fin over a long body with a tail, 22 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 7/5/4/4/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 92nd co-play prompt (be a shark together — one hand on top of the head like a shark fin saying 'fin… fin!', swim side to side saying 'swish… swish!' fast then slow, make a big shark mouth with your arms and chomp saying 'chomp… chomp!', then swim slow and rest like a sleepy shark; take turns; pretend only, no real water, real sharks are look, don't touch; at SeaWorld, watch the sharks swim past the glass together). Shark-play research: at 2, the shark dance form is a big arm-jaw chomp plus a little finger chomp and a fin on the head (the 'become the shark' move); 'chomp' is the entry word, and 'swim fast or slow?' is the tempo contrast; the arm-jaw chomp is distinct from Crab's hand-claw snap and Star's finger open/shut. Timed to the SeaWorld trip — the family visits SeaWorld tomorrow (Fri Nov 13), so the tower lands the day before, the same trip-timing as Dolphin (SeaWorld-eve). v2.95 (2026-11-12, morning run): 94th tower 'Brick' (three studs over four solid bands, 34 blocks, 7 clusters sizes 7/7/7/7/2/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 91st co-play prompt (build with real bricks together — stack big bricks saying 'up… up… up!', count the studs — one, two, three! — then knock it down saying 'crash… down!', then sit down and stack it back up slowly and rest; take turns adding a brick; big bricks only — little LEGO bricks are too small for little hands, grown-up builds with those; at LEGOLAND, look for the giant bricks together). Brick-play research: at 2, stacking and pulling apart big bricks builds fine motor and hand-eye coordination; building it up and smashing it down is the fun part (the knock-down is the payoff); counting studs and sorting by colour is early math; Duplo-sized bricks are made for small hands with no small parts. Dolphin-play research: the leap is the dolphin's signature movement toddlers copy (arms together, arch up, jump/splash down); clicks and whistles are the dolphin sounds, and the echolocation clap game (dolphin claps twice, fish answer) is a copyable clap-exchange at 2; dolphins swim together in pods and help each other — the social form is togetherness. Timed to the LEGOLAND trip — SeaWorld is Fri Nov 13, so the tower lands the day before the park visit, the same trip-timing as Airplane (flight day), Dragon (park-eve), and Pirate (park day). v2.93 (2026-11-11, evening run): 92nd tower 'Pirate' (green hat tip over a red brim, a face with a blue patch band, a green shirt, on two blue boots, 31 blocks, 7 clusters sizes 7/7/7/3/3/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 89th co-play prompt (play pirates together — put on a paper pirate hat or a bandana saying 'arrr… arrr!', rock side to side like you're sailing saying 'sail… sail!', then follow the treasure map: hide a favourite toy under a pillow together and find it saying 'treasure… found it!'; take turns being the captain; no toy swords — a soft parrot on your shoulder works instead, and a grown-up hides the treasure). Pirate-play research: the first treasure hunt is the toddler pirate form (hide one favourite toy, help him find it) and the map is what makes it a pirate hunt rather than a hiding game, keeping it distinct from the Stocking tower's hide-and-find; 'arrr'/'ahoy' are the sound words at the moment of motion; the paper hat is the one-prop costume and toy swords stay out. Airplane-play research: arms-out flying plus takeoff-and-landing is gross-motor work (balance, coordination, spatial awareness) that teaches up/down and fast/slow; 'vroom' and 'up, up, up!' are the entry words modelled at the moment of motion; pretend flying gives a sense of control and adventure, which can ease travel-day nerves. v2.90 (2026-11-10, evening run): 89th tower 'Elf' (floppy pointed hat over ears and a face, a body with a belt, on two boots, 24 blocks, 8 clusters sizes 6/4/3/3/2/2/2/2, all 4 colours, no singletons, 0 canonical duplicates) + 86th co-play prompt (play Santa's workshop together — put on a pointy elf hat, a paper cone works, then make a toy for your teddy by stacking real blocks, tap it together, wrap it in paper and put it in the bag; take turns being the elf who makes it and Santa who checks it; a paper cone or a soft hat is the whole costume, no little bells on shoes, grown-up holds any real tools). Present-play research: tearing wrapping paper is multisensory cause-and-effect (crinkle, resistance, rip) that toddlers often love more than the gift itself; it builds fine motor (pincer grasp, bilateral hold-and-pull) and object permanence ('what's inside?' guessing); wrapping together is a giving moment, kept simple and safe. v2.86 (2026-11-09, afternoon run): 85th tower 'Stocking' (cuff over a narrow leg on a foot that juts to one side, 18 blocks, 4 clusters sizes 8/4/2/4, all 4 colours, no singletons) + 82nd co-play prompt (hang a stocking — or a big sock! — on a hook, hide a big soft toy inside saying 'where did it go?', reach in and pull it out saying 'peek-a-boo… there it is!', taking turns hiding and finding; only big soft toys go in, no coins, no small balls, no hard candy, grown-up does the hanging and checks what's inside). Stocking-play research: 'what's in the stocking?' is a guessing game (touch/smell/sound, then reveal, then reverse roles) that builds vocabulary, inference, and senses; hiding and finding is object permanence in action — start partially hidden, ask 'where did it go?', answer with positive surprise; stocking stuffers for under-3s must be too big to swallow (AAP/CPSC small-parts test). v2.85 (2026-11-09, morning run): 84th tower 'Christmas Tree' (star tip over tiered bands on a trunk, 16 blocks, 5 clusters sizes 4/4/2/2/4, all 4 colours, no singletons) + 81st co-play prompt (decorate a real tree together — hang big soft ornaments on the low branches, count them — one, two, three! — then put the star on top together and step back to look; soft felt/wood/plastic ornaments only, low branches, no glass or sharp hooks, grown-up handles lights and cords).
